14595.title: Data Jurisdiction
14595.heading: Data Jurisdiction
14595.content:
Data jurisdiction identifies the laws and regulatory authority that apply to data and the systems or people handling it. A cloud provider, user, application host, storage location, and support team may each be located in a different country.

The applicable jurisdiction should therefore be established before a service is purchased, not inferred only from the consumer's location. Geographic movement caused by elastic provisioning must remain compatible with the service's legal and compliance requirements.

14598.title: Data Integrity
14598.heading: Data Integrity
14598.content:
Data integrity is the property that information remains accurate, complete, and consistent with its intended use. An accidental change, deliberate substitution, transmission error, or unauthorized modification can all violate integrity.

Integrity must be protected across the full data journey, including endpoints, communication channels, active processing, storage, backup, and archival. Authentication of endpoints, encryption, checksums, monitoring, and controlled modification each address a different part of that journey.

14601.sourceSearchName: data integrity verification data integrity verification
14601.title: Data Integrity Verification
14601.heading: Data Integrity Verification
14601.content:
Data integrity verification checks that information remains the same across storage, transmission, or processing. A sender can calculate a [[Cryptographic Hash Function|cryptographic hash]], and a recipient can recompute it and compare the result with a trusted original digest.

Matching hashes support evidence that the data was not altered, but an unkeyed hash alone does not establish who supplied it. Authentication or a signature is required when origin matters as well as content.

14604.title: Data Integration
14604.heading: Data Integration
14604.content:
Data integration allows applications or services to exchange and jointly use information. It requires both a compatible representation and a shared understanding of what the represented fields mean.

Two files can use the same format while containing incompatible data models, and two services can describe the same business concept in different formats. A [[Common Data Model]] plus agreed encodings and validation rules makes the exchange interpretable rather than merely transferable.

In an evidence pipeline, integration combines extracted records before cleaning, storage, and exploration. The join rules and entity matches determine which observations are treated as belonging together, so integration decisions become part of the evidence behind a conclusion.

14607.sourceSearchName: data in use data in use
14607.title: Data in Use
14607.heading: Data in Use
14607.content:
Data in use is active information being read, changed, calculated, or otherwise processed by a user, application, or system. It may be protected during storage and transmission yet become exposed when an authorized process makes it usable.

Authorization, process isolation, monitoring, endpoint security, and careful handling of temporary copies help protect this state. [[Data Loss Prevention]] must include active use rather than treating encryption at rest as complete protection.

14610.sourceSearchName: data in transit data in transit
14610.title: Data in Transit
14610.heading: Data in Transit
14610.content:
Data in transit is information moving between systems, services, or network locations. During transmission it can be observed, altered, redirected, replayed, or blocked if the communication path is not adequately protected.

An [[Encrypted Communication Channel]] can provide confidentiality and integrity for this state, while endpoint authentication helps establish who is communicating. These protections complement the separate controls needed for [[Data at Rest]] and [[Data in Process]].

14613.sourceSearchName: data in process data in process
14613.title: Data in Process
14613.heading: Data in Process
14613.content:
Data in process is information actively being used by a program or computing device. Processing may require plaintext values in memory, so protections that secure [[Data at Rest]] or [[Data in Transit]] do not automatically cover this state.

Process isolation, memory protection, least privilege, trusted execution, and careful application design reduce exposure while data is active. Considering all [[Data Security States]] prevents storage or transport encryption from creating a false sense of complete protection.

14616.sourceSearchName: data in motion data in motion
14616.title: Data in Motion
14616.heading: Data in Motion
14616.content:
Data in motion is information being transported between endpoints over a communication channel. It can be exposed to interception, alteration, substitution, loss, or delivery to an unintended party while it moves.

Secure channels, endpoint authentication, encryption, checksums, and appropriate message delivery controls protect different aspects of the transfer. The protection should persist across every network boundary in the data's end-to-end journey.

14619.title: Data Fragmentation
14619.heading: Data Fragmentation
14619.content:
Data fragmentation divides a relation or dataset into pieces that can be stored and processed separately. Horizontal fragmentation separates rows, while vertical fragmentation separates groups of columns while retaining a way to reconstruct the original relation.

Distribution can improve parallelism and locality, but queries that cross fragments pay communication and coordination costs.

14621.title: Data Filtering

14622.title: Data Filtering
14622.heading: Data Filtering
14622.content:
Data filtering restricts a result set to records matching a supplied condition. Applying the filter on the server before paging reduces the number of rows counted, transferred, and displayed.

A client search control can pass a filter value to an API, which composes it into an [[IQueryable]] before execution. Input and field choices must be constrained so filtering does not introduce a [[SQL Injection]] path.

14625.title: Data Extraction
14625.heading: Data Extraction
14625.content:
Data extraction retrieves relevant records from source systems so they can enter an analytical pipeline. Sources may differ in structure, access method, update rate, and meaning, so extraction must preserve enough provenance to interpret later results.

Selecting what to extract already shapes the evidence. Missing systems, inaccessible fields, and inconsistent collection practices can produce a partial view before modeling begins.

14628.title: Data Discretization
14628.heading: Data Discretization
14628.content:
Data discretization converts a continuous or highly varied attribute into a finite set of intervals or categories. The representation can reduce complexity, support algorithms that expect discrete inputs, and make patterns easier to interpret.

The interval boundaries determine how much information is preserved. A scalable discretizer must find useful cut points without requiring repeated full-data operations that become impractical on large datasets.

14631.sourceSearchName: data disclosure paradox data disclosure paradox
14631.title: Data Disclosure Paradox
14631.heading: Data Disclosure Paradox
14631.content:
The data disclosure paradox claims that a prospective buyer cannot value information without seeing it, yet disclosure gives away what the seller hoped to sell. It is often used to argue that data markets need property-like protection.

For large datasets, the problem is weaker than it first appears. Samples, descriptions, contractual safeguards, and the difference between inspecting a portion and obtaining the complete resource can support valuation without transferring the full value.

14634.title: Data Cube
14634.heading: Data Cube
14634.content:
A data cube is a multidimensional arrangement of measures indexed by analytic dimensions. It makes common summaries and cross-sections efficient to retrieve from a large body of organizational data.

Users can slice, dice, pivot, drill down, or roll up the cube to explore patterns at different resolutions. These operations guide questions and preparation but do not replace statistical or machine-learning validation.

14637.title: Data Cleansing
14637.heading: Data Cleansing
14637.content:
Data cleansing analyzes fields, corrects or removes erroneous values, fills missing information where justified, and enforces domain and business rules. It is the activity used to improve data quality before and during analysis.

Cleaning is continuous because codes, systems, and real-world conditions change. Every correction should preserve provenance and distinguish error repair from deletion of a valid rare case.

Within a decision pipeline, cleansing occurs alongside extraction, transformation, integration, and storage. Each correction or exclusion changes the evidence available to later exploration and visualization, so its rules must be tied to the meaning and intended use of the data.

The decision couples market prices with workload forecasts, storage limits, carbon goals, and the cost of violating service commitments.

14643.title: Data Cache
14643.heading: Data Cache
14643.content:
A data cache keeps a reusable result closer to the application so repeated requests do not always query the database. In-memory caching can shorten a read path for data whose temporary reuse is acceptable.

Caching introduces a freshness decision. The application needs a key, an expiration policy, and a reasoned response to writes so that lower latency does not silently serve unsuitable old data.

14646.sourceSearchName: data binning thresholds data binning thresholds
14646.title: Data Binning Thresholds
14646.heading: Data Binning Thresholds
14646.content:
Binning transforms a numeric field into ranges, such as grouping customer ages into age bands. It can make a coarse distinction more useful than treating every adjacent value as substantively different.

The thresholds are a domain choice. A poorly placed boundary can separate very similar cases or conceal a distinction important to the target. Data transformation therefore needs domain knowledge, exploratory checks, and sometimes trial-and-error evaluation rather than assuming that a convenient round-number cut is neutral.

14649.sourceSearchName: data at rest data at rest
14649.title: Data at Rest
14649.heading: Data at Rest
14649.content:
Data at rest is inactive or intermittently used data stored in a digital medium, including disks, cloud storage, backups, and archives. Its storage location may persist long after the application that created it has stopped running.

Protection can include encryption, access control, retention limits, integrity verification, and secure destruction. Backup and archival copies must be included because protecting only the primary store leaves other copies exposed.

The source distinguishes stored data from [[Data in Transit]] and [[Data in Process]]. At-rest protection can combine encryption with access control, but key management remains critical because a protected store becomes readable wherever its decryption keys are exposed.

14652.title: Data as a Nonrivalrous Good
14652.heading: Data as a Nonrivalrous Good
14652.content:
Data are nonrivalrous because one party can use a copy without preventing another party from using the same information. Copying therefore differs from taking a physical object whose possession is exclusive.

Nonrivalry complicates the justification and scope of a [[Data Ownership Right]]. Exclusive control may create incentives or bargaining power, but it can also restrict socially useful reuse without being necessary to preserve the original holder's use.

14655.title: Data Archive
14655.heading: Data Archive
14655.content:
A data archive preserves information that is no longer used regularly but must be retained for historical, regulatory, or compliance reasons. Search and retrieval over long retention periods matter more than immediate operational restoration.

An archive differs from a backup, whose purpose is rapid recovery of changing day-to-day data. Backup retention is commonly measured in weeks or months, while archival retention can extend for years or decades.

14658.title: Data Annotation
14658.heading: Data Annotation
14658.content:
A data annotation is metadata attached to a model member to express mapping or validation rules. In an Entity Framework Core entity, annotations can identify keys, required values, lengths, or other constraints that cannot be inferred sufficiently from naming conventions alone.

Annotations supplement [[Convention over Configuration]]. They keep simple rules close to the entity definition, while more complicated mapping remains available through explicit model configuration.

14661.title: Data Analyst
14661.heading: Data Analyst
14661.content:
A data analyst converts organized data into summaries, comparisons, and explanations that answer defined questions. The work emphasizes correct measures, suitable visualizations, and interpretation within the problem domain.

In the book's capability progression, analysis builds on sound data preparation and precedes the broader pattern discovery associated with a [[Data Miner]].

14664.title: Dapper
14664.heading: Dapper
14664.content:
Dapper is a lightweight .NET data-access library that executes SQL and maps parameters and result columns to typed objects. The application retains direct control over its queries instead of expressing them through a larger object-relational model.

This makes SQL visible and concise while still removing repetitive command and mapping code. The repository remains responsible for query design, connection use, and the shape returned to the application.

14667.sourceSearchName: dapper multiple results dapper multiple results
14667.title: Dapper Multiple Results
14667.heading: Dapper Multiple Results
14667.content:
Dapper can execute several SQL result sets in one database command and expose a reader for consuming them in order. A repository can retrieve parent records and related child records in one round trip, then associate them in memory.

This avoids the duplicated columns of a large join while still controlling round-trip count. The code must keep the result-set order and mapping contract synchronized with the SQL batch.

14670.sourceSearchName: dapper multi mapping dapper multi mapping
14670.title: Dapper Multi-Mapping
14670.heading: Dapper Multi-Mapping
14670.content:
Dapper multi-mapping divides columns from one joined row into multiple object types and uses a mapping function to assemble their relationship. It supports loading a parent and related records from one query rather than issuing a new query for every parent.

Because a join repeats parent columns for each child, the mapping code must identify existing parent objects and attach each child to the correct collection. The reduced round trips are exchanged for more deliberate assembly logic.

14673.title: Dangling Node
14673.heading: Dangling Node
14673.content:
A dangling node in PageRank is a page with incoming links but no outgoing links. Its row in the [[Hyperlink Matrix]] contains only zeros, so rank flows into the node without being redistributed.

Uncorrected dangling nodes drain the total rank during repeated multiplication. The [[Random Surfer Model]] treats a surfer at such a dead end as able to jump to any page, replacing the zero row with equal transition probabilities.

14676.sourceSearchName: cynical software satisfaction cynical software satisfaction
14676.title: Cynical Software Satisfaction
14676.heading: Cynical Software Satisfaction
14676.content:
Cynical satisfaction occurs when users trust enough of a product’s claims to keep using it while expecting bugs, workarounds, weak support, and security problems. Their commitment is shallow and may disappear when a better option arrives.

This level often results from pressure to release quickly and shift liability to customers. It produces functional software without the disciplined care needed for durable trust.

14679.title: Daily Scrum
14679.heading: Daily Scrum
14679.content:
The Daily Scrum is a roughly fifteen-minute Development Team event for inspecting progress toward the [[Sprint Goal]] and coordinating the next day of work. Members surface progress, intended work, and impediments that affect the team's plan.

It is not a status report to a manager or a place to solve every problem. Detailed problem-solving follows with only the people who need to participate.

14682.title: Damping
14682.heading: Damping
14682.content: Damping removes mechanical energy from an oscillator through resistive forces, causing amplitude to decrease with time. Light damping leaves several oscillations before decay; critical damping returns the system to equilibrium as quickly as possible without oscillation; overdamping returns more slowly. Damping also broadens and lowers the response near [[Resonance]].

14685.title: Cypress
14685.heading: Cypress
14685.content:
Cypress is the browser testing tool used in the book to automate an end-to-end React application scenario. A test visits the running application, locates interface elements, performs user actions, and asserts the resulting visible behavior.

Because the scenario crosses client, API, and data behavior, its environment and starting state must be controlled. A failure can indicate a broken workflow even when every isolated unit test still passes.

14688.title: D-Stream
14688.heading: D-Stream
14688.content:
D-Stream maps incoming points to grid cells, updates cell densities over time, and periodically clusters adjacent dense cells. Density decay lets cell states change among dense, transitional, and sparse as the stream evolves.

The grid makes updates independent of the total number of past observations and can describe irregular regions through connected cells. Fixed resolution and periodic adjustment can delay or distort rapidly changing fine-scale patterns.

Cylindrical fin parameterization defines radial and axial dimensions, base placement, and any internal channel through reusable parameters. Cylinders, blocks, work planes, partitions, and deletion operations can then construct the final solid.

Named dimensions make the relationship between surface area, material volume, and heat path auditable. They also let a family of cylindrical designs be rebuilt without manually editing every geometric feature.

14697.title: Cyclic Quadrilateral
14697.heading: Cyclic Quadrilateral
14697.content: A cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on one circle. Opposite interior angles are supplementary because each is an inscribed angle intercepting arcs that together complete the circle. Conversely, a quadrilateral with supplementary opposite angles can be inscribed in a circle.

14700.title: Cyclic Module
14700.heading: Cyclic Module
14700.content:
A cyclic module is generated by one element m. The map R → Rm sending r to rm is surjective, with kernel Ann(m), so Rm is isomorphic to R/Ann(m).

This description connects elements to ideals. A prime p is an [[Associated Prime]] of M exactly when M contains a cyclic submodule isomorphic to R/p.

14703.title: Cyclic Group
14703.heading: Cyclic Group
14703.content:
A cyclic group consists of all integer powers, or integer multiples, of one element. It is written ⟨a⟩, where a is a generator.

Every cyclic group is abelian, and every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic.

Cycles can expose specialized passes for compositing light and motion. A vector pass stores image-space movement for effects such as vector blur, while a UV pass preserves mapping information that can help change textures after rendering.

A shadow pass isolates cast shadows so their color or intensity can be changed independently. These passes preserve choices that would otherwise require the scene to be rendered again.

14709.title: Cycle Time
14709.heading: Cycle Time
14709.content:
Cycle time is the elapsed time from when work actually begins on an item until that item is completed. It includes active work and waiting that occurs after the start.

Tracking cycle time reveals how quickly the system finishes what it starts. Smaller batches, fewer handoffs, and lower work in progress can reduce it by limiting queues and feedback delay.

14712.heading: Cycle in a Chain Complex

An n-cycle is an element of the kernel of the differential dₙ: Cₙ → Cₙ₋₁. It is sent to zero by the next map in a [[Chain Complex]].

Every [[Boundary in a Chain Complex]] is a cycle, but a cycle need not be a boundary. The quotient of cycles by boundaries is the n-th [[Homology Group]].

14715.title: Cybersickness
14715.heading: Cybersickness
14715.content:
Cybersickness is discomfort associated with virtual or three-dimensional systems and is symptomatically similar to motion sickness. It is also called simulator sickness or VR sickness in particular contexts.

A leading explanation is conflict among sensory signals. For example, a [[Visual Display]] may indicate movement while the vestibular system indicates that the body is stationary. Poor [[Feedback Compliance]], [[Latency]], low update rates, or misregistration can intensify the mismatch.

Symptoms can include headache, blurred vision, dizziness, disorientation, and nausea. Because susceptibility differs among people, evaluation should measure user comfort and provide rest or stopping procedures rather than relying only on system performance.

14718.title: Cybersecurity Risk Assessment
14718.heading: Cybersecurity Risk Assessment
14718.content:
A cybersecurity risk assessment identifies valued assets, relevant [[Cyber Threat|threats]], exploitable [[Cyber Vulnerability|vulnerabilities]], existing controls, and the likely impact of harmful events. It turns a broad concern about security into a prioritized account of what could happen and why it matters.

The result supports decisions about treatment, acceptance, transfer, or avoidance of risk. Because systems and threats change, assessment is a continuing process rather than a one-time checklist.

14721.title: Cybersecurity Integrity
14721.heading: Cybersecurity Integrity
14721.content:
Cybersecurity integrity is the trustworthiness and reliability of systems and data. A user needs evidence that a system has not been compromised and that information has not been changed without authorization.

The source separates [[System Integrity Verification]] from [[Data Integrity Verification]] because trustworthy data depends on the environment that stores and processes it. Hashes, secure boot, identity checks, and protected storage provide different parts of that evidence.

14724.sourceSearchName: cybersecurity goal model cybersecurity goal model
14724.title: Cybersecurity Goal Model
14724.heading: Cybersecurity Goal Model
14724.content:
The source organizes cybersecurity around six goals: [[Cybersecurity Confidentiality]], [[Cybersecurity Integrity]], [[Cybersecurity Availability]], [[Authentication]], [[Authorization]], and [[Nonrepudiation]]. The first three form the commonly recognized confidentiality-integrity-availability group, while the other three make identity, access, and source evidence explicit.

These goals describe desired outcomes rather than particular products. One incident can damage several at once, so controls should be judged by the security properties they preserve across people, systems, applications, and data.

14727.title: Cybersecurity Confidentiality
14727.heading: Cybersecurity Confidentiality
14727.content:
Confidentiality keeps information secret from parties that are not authorized to receive it. Access restrictions can limit who reaches the information, while [[Encryption]] converts it into an unreadable representation for anyone without the required key.

Confidentiality resembles privacy but is framed as a security property of information and communication. It must be protected while data is stored, transmitted, and processed, because disclosure at any state defeats the goal.

14730.title: Cybersecurity Availability
14730.heading: Cybersecurity Availability
14730.content:
Availability ensures that information and services are usable by the right people when they are needed. A denial-of-service attack violates this goal by exhausting or disabling the resources that legitimate users require.

Redundant servers, backups, resilient networks, and recovery plans preserve availability when a component fails or is attacked. Security controls must also avoid causing unnecessary downtime while responding to another security problem.

14733.title: Cybersecurity Anomaly Detection
14733.heading: Cybersecurity Anomaly Detection
14733.content:
Cybersecurity anomaly detection identifies activity that differs materially from a [[Behavioral Security Baseline]]. It can expose unknown attacks, compromised accounts, unusual data movement, or system faults that lack a known malicious signature.

An anomaly is evidence for investigation, not proof of attack. Effective detection balances sensitivity with context so that normal variation does not overwhelm responders and subtle harmful behavior is not absorbed into the baseline.

Cybernetics studies communication and control through feedback in machines, organisms, and organizations. Norbert Wiener developed its mathematical foundations while considering how a system could track a moving target despite noise and evasive behavior.

Feedback compares observed behavior with a goal and adjusts subsequent action. The concept influenced computing even though it did not depend on the stored-program digital architecture.

Cyber weaponization prepares a malicious capability for a chosen target, while delivery brings it to the target through a message, website, removable medium, network service, or another channel. Together they connect reconnaissance to an attempted compromise.

In the [[Cyber Kill Chain]], filtering, safe content handling, user verification, and endpoint controls can interrupt delivery before the payload reaches [[Cyber Exploitation and Installation]].

14742.title: Cyberattack Attribution
14742.heading: Cyberattack Attribution
14742.content:
Cyberattack attribution is the process of determining who is responsible for an attack. Technical traces can reveal infrastructure, tools, timing, or methods, but attackers can reuse code, route activity through other systems, and deliberately plant misleading evidence.

Attribution therefore combines technical evidence with context and intelligence about a possible [[Threat Actor]]. The source cautions that identifying an apparent origin is not the same as establishing responsibility with certainty.

14745.title: Cyber Vulnerability
14745.heading: Cyber Vulnerability
14745.content:
A cyber vulnerability is a weakness that can be exploited to violate a system's security goals. It may arise from software, configuration, architecture, procedure, or human behavior rather than from code alone.

A vulnerability does not by itself determine harm. [[Cyber Risk Formula]] relates it to the relevant [[Cyber Threat]] and the impact of a successful event, helping defenders prioritize weaknesses instead of treating every flaw as equally urgent.

14748.title: Cyber Threat
14748.heading: Cyber Threat
14748.content:
A cyber threat is a circumstance or actor capable of causing harm to an information system or the assets it supports. A threat represents potential danger; it becomes an attack when someone takes action to exploit an opportunity.

Keeping threats distinct from [[Cyber Vulnerability]] and [[Security Risk]] makes analysis clearer. A system may contain a weakness without an active adversary, while a threat may exist without a usable path into that system.

14754.title: Cyber Reconnaissance
14754.heading: Cyber Reconnaissance
14754.content:
Cyber reconnaissance is the information-gathering stage of the [[Cyber Kill Chain]]. An attacker studies potential targets, technologies, people, relationships, and exposed services to find a promising path for later action.

Reconnaissance may combine public information with active probing. Reducing unnecessary exposure and monitoring unusual discovery behavior can make targeting harder or reveal an operation before malware is delivered.

The cyber kill chain models an intrusion as a sequence: [[Cyber Reconnaissance]], [[Cyber Weaponization and Delivery]], [[Cyber Exploitation and Installation]], [[Cyber Command and Control]], and [[Cyber Actions on Objectives]]. The stages describe how an attacker moves from preparation to the intended effect.

Defenders can use the model to place opportunities for detection and disruption throughout an operation. Breaking any necessary stage can prevent later objectives even if an earlier control failed.

14760.heading: Cyber Exploitation and Installation

Cyber exploitation uses a weakness to execute an attacker's intended action, and installation establishes malicious code or access on the compromised system. The stages may occur close together, but one describes gaining execution while the other creates a foothold.

Within the [[Cyber Kill Chain]], patching, isolation, least privilege, and host monitoring can block or expose these stages before the attacker establishes [[Cyber Command and Control]].

14763.heading: Cyber Deception Outcome
14763.content:
A cyber deception outcome occurs when an attacker causes users or systems to accept false information, identities, or states as genuine. The harm is not limited to secret theft or interrupted service; corrupted trust can redirect decisions while systems appear available.

Authentication, integrity verification, provenance evidence, and independent confirmation help resist this outcome. Framing deception explicitly extends [[Outcome-Based Cyber Defense]] beyond confidentiality and availability alone.

14766.heading: Cyber Command and Control
14766.content:
Cyber command and control is the communication channel through which an attacker directs a compromised system and receives information from it. This connection turns an isolated foothold into a remotely managed part of an operation.

Blocking or detecting command traffic can disrupt the [[Cyber Kill Chain]] after installation. Network monitoring, destination controls, behavioral analysis, and [[Extrusion Detection]] can reveal communication that ordinary permitted traffic might otherwise conceal.

14769.heading: Cyber Actions on Objectives
14769.content:
Cyber actions on objectives are the effects an attacker pursues after establishing access, such as stealing data, disrupting service, changing information, surveilling users, or expanding control. They are the final outcome-oriented stage of the [[Cyber Kill Chain]].

Defenders should identify these likely outcomes in advance. Controls that preserve essential functions, constrain privileges, detect data leaving the environment, and support recovery can reduce harm even after intrusion.

14772.title: Cutscene
14772.heading: Cutscene
14772.content:
A cutscene is a section of a game devoted primarily to showing noninteractive story material. It can use animation, dialogue, still images, or other presentation and often appears between playable sections as an intermission.

Cutscenes can provide context and rest from [[Game Resistance|resistance]], but they place playing and watching beside one another rather than fully integrating them. Requiring timed input inside a cutscene adds exertion without necessarily making its choices meaningful.

14775.heading: Cut-and-Stack Time Plot
14775.content: A cut-and-stack time plot divides a long time axis into overlapping segments and places those segments in aligned rows. It preserves an aspect ratio selected through [[Banking to 45 Degrees]] without producing an extremely wide or shallow figure. Small overlaps help the reader continue a trajectory across row boundaries. The layout improves local slope perception, but the discontinuous horizontal arrangement makes very long-range timing comparisons less immediate.

14787.content:
A custom accelerator implements a targeted computation with hardware resources and a data path specialized for its operations. Removing general-purpose instruction overhead can improve throughput, latency, or energy efficiency.

The benefit is limited by host communication, memory bandwidth, unsupported cases, and the cost of changing the design when the algorithm or data representation evolves.

14790.heading: Cumulative Sequence Feature
14790.content:
A cumulative sequence feature summarizes all matches of a pattern across an entire sequence. Binary presence and total occurrence count are common cumulative mappings.

This produces a fixed-length representation independent of sequence length and match positions. It is efficient for standard learners but discards when events occurred and how their occurrences were distributed.

14793.title: Cumulative Hazard
14793.heading: Cumulative Hazard
14793.content:
Cumulative hazard accumulates instantaneous event risk over time. It starts at zero and increases as risk is experienced, providing a complementary representation to the declining survival probability.

Plotting cumulative hazards by group helps assess the [[Proportional Hazards Assumption]]. Curves that remain roughly proportional or parallel support a constant relative effect more than curves that cross or diverge irregularly.

Cultured meat water use includes process water, cleaning, cooling, culture medium, and water embodied in agricultural or industrial inputs. Avoiding animal drinking water and feed crops can reduce demand compared with some livestock systems.

A complete estimate must include facility sanitation and upstream ingredient production rather than counting only liquid present in the bioreactor.

A cumulative distribution function gives, for every value, the probability or proportion of observations less than or equal to that value. It compresses an ordered collection into a monotone description of where its values lie.

Differences between two cumulative values give the probability of an interval. A [[Quantile]] reverses the relationship by starting with a cumulative probability and returning the corresponding value.

Repeated evidence can stabilize assignments that recur across runs. Alignment errors and dominance by many nearly identical inputs can distort the vote, so ensemble diversity and component weighting must be considered.

14826.title: Cultural Interactivity
14826.heading: Cultural Interactivity
14826.content:
Cultural interactivity is the long-timescale reflection and dialogue a game provokes about cultural values, assumptions, or practices. It may continue after play and outside the game's immediate [[Magic Circle]].

Unlike fast action loops, its feedback may appear through conversation, interpretation, and later behavior. It can therefore become an outer loop around [[Social Interactivity]] and the player's evolving meaning of the experience.

14829.content:
Color meaning is not universal. A hue can suggest danger, celebration, purity, authority, nature, or mourning depending on culture, surrounding symbols, and the situation in which the player encounters it.

Environment artists should treat associations as hypotheses to test with the target audience. Shape, value contrast, text, and sound should reinforce critical signals so progress or hazards do not depend on color perception alone.

14832.heading: Culture Medium Cost
14832.content:
Culture medium cost can dominate the price of cell-based products because large cell populations repeatedly consume nutrient and signaling mixtures. The source cites estimates in which medium accounts for more than half and potentially nearly all tissue-production cost.

Food applications can reduce purity requirements and explore recycling, but reused medium must not accumulate harmful waste or contamination.

14835.title: Cultivated Meat
14835.heading: Cultivated Meat
14835.content:
Cultivated meat is edible animal tissue grown from cultured cells outside a whole animal. Muscle cells are central, but fat, connective tissue, vascular cells, matrix, and processing contribute to the resulting product.

Manufacturing must expand enormous cell numbers, use food-compatible inputs, and reproduce enough nutrition, texture, appearance, aroma, flavor, and cooking behavior to serve as meat.

14838.title: Cultivated Leather
14838.heading: Cultivated Leather
14838.content:
Cultivated leather is a leather-like material produced from cells and their secreted collagen rather than from a complete animal hide. Fibroblast sheets can be layered, matured, and processed with adapted tanning methods.

Uniformity and predetermined shape reduce waste, but collagen content, thickness, tear strength, and compatibility with stitching must reach the demands of finished goods.

14841.title: Cube
14841.heading: Cube
14841.content:
The cube of a quantity is its third power:

$$a^3=a\cdot a\cdot a.$$

The name corresponds to the volume of a geometric cube with edge length (a). Unlike a square, a cube preserves the sign of a real number because it contains an odd number of factors: ((-a)^3=-a^3). Reversing the operation uses a [[Cube Root]]. Cubes also form reusable expansion and factorization patterns such as the [[Sum of Cubes Identity]].

14844.title: Cube Root
14844.heading: Cube Root
14844.content:
A cube root of (a) is a number whose [[Cube]] equals (a):

$$b=\sqrt[3]{a}\quad\text{when}\quad b^3=a.$$

For example, (sqrt[3]{27}=3) and (sqrt[3]{-27}=-3). Because cubing preserves sign and is one-to-one on real numbers, every real number has exactly one real cube root. The index (3) is written on the radical symbol, unlike the usually omitted index (2) of a [[Square Root]].

14847.title: Cube Projection UV Mapping
14847.heading: Cube Projection UV Mapping
14847.content:
Cube Projection assigns faces according to their orientation toward six box-like projection directions. It quickly maps buildings, crates, and other forms whose major surfaces align approximately with perpendicular axes.

Cube size changes how the projection fills texture space, while aspect and bounds settings control fitting. Curved or diagonally oriented regions may split or distort, so the resulting islands still need inspection and adjustment.
